issues.explanation: 'People cycling' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile for a refugee trauma presentation when the other triggers are funerals/graves and car sounds, and there are no corresponding memory or appraisal items suggesting bicycles or a cycling-related trauma cue. This trigger looks clinically disconnected from the stated trauma context and the rest of the network.

'I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. In an older married male refugee with severe PTSD symptoms, self-harm can occur, but here it is the only extreme behavioral regulation item and is unsupported by the other selected strategies, memories, or appraisals. It appears clinically out of pattern relative to the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation.

vignette:
Rajesh had not spoken of the journey in over forty years. When he tried, the words would not come; the memory existed as a series of fractured sensations-the deafening crack of gunfire, the smell of diesel and damp earth, the sight of his younger brother's body crumpling beside a checkpoint while a policeman shouted in a language that was almost familiar. He could feel the cold metal of the truck bed against his back, hear the grinding of gears, see the dust rising in clouds, but he could not arrange these pieces into a story that made sense. The fragments felt more real than anything that had happened since-more vivid than the birth of his children, more present than the clay spinning beneath his hands on the wheel.

For years after arriving in America, Rajesh had thrown himself into his pottery. The work gave him a rhythm, a way to be still. But as he aged, something shifted. A car backfiring in the street would send his heart racing before his mind could catch up. The sound was not a memory-it was a return. Each time his body reacted before his mind could catch up, he felt the quiet confirmation that he was no longer capable of the steady life he had built - that something essential in him had broken beyond repair. He would find himself scanning the parking lot, checking the shadows, though he could not say what he was looking for. When a neighbor's funeral procession passed his house, he felt a wave of dread so heavy he had to sit down. He began to believe he was no longer capable of the quiet, steady work that had once defined him. Once he had concluded that he was permanently diminished, almost anything could confirm it - a customer's complaint, a missed delivery, even a glance from a stranger that might mean nothing but felt like everything. The slightest upset-a customer complaining about a glaze, a missed delivery-felt catastrophic. He had come to believe that he had to be especially careful, because you never knew what could happen next. That conviction - that the world was fundamentally dangerous and he was too fragile to meet it - fed directly into the fractured sensations, pulling him back to the checkpoint with a force that felt like proof of his own helplessness.

The vigilance was exhausting, but letting it go felt impossible. Rajesh started avoiding anything that might stir hope or happiness, because those feelings seemed dangerous-they made him vulnerable, made him forget to watch. He also avoided any hint of disagreement, even with his wife over something as trivial as dinner. A raised voice, even in jest, made his stomach clench. He began checking his surroundings constantly, scanning the kiln room before he entered, glancing over his shoulder when he walked to the post office. These strategies briefly calmed him, but they also confirmed his worst fear: that he could not cope with even ordinary life. The more he avoided, the more he felt he had to avoid, and the more the fractured memories intruded-not as narrative, but as sensation, pulling him back to that truck bed. Each retreat from the world added a new layer of evidence that he was too weak to manage ordinary life, deepening the belief that had driven him into hiding in the first place.

The police presence in his town became unbearable. A patrol car parked near his studio would ruin his concentration for hours. The sight of a uniform made his hands shake, and he would retreat inside, locking the door, certain that something terrible was about to happen. He had stopped attending community events, stopped visiting the temple, stopped taking his grandchildren to the park. The avoidance had drawn a map of the past around him: every street he no longer walked, every conversation he could no longer hold, every place he kept at a distance became a reminder of what had happened and what he had become. His wife had begun to worry; she said he was disappearing into himself. Rajesh knew she was right, but he could not explain why. The fragments of the past had become a prison, and every avoidance made the walls thicker.

What finally brought him to seek help was a morning in early spring. A hearse passed his studio slowly, and he found himself on the floor, clutching a half-formed bowl, unable to breathe. He understood then that his life had become smaller than the space between his hands. He was afraid of what he might become if he did not find a way to speak the unspeakable-but he was equally afraid that if he did, the pieces would never fit back together.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that triggers (e.g., car backfiring, police presence) cause or lead to negative appraisals (e.g., ‘he could not cope’).
No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals cause or lead to intrusive memory; the memory intrudes without being driven by appraisals.
No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals cause or lead to triggers; triggers appear independently.

No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies (avoidance, checking) cause or lead to negative appraisals; the text says strategies ‘confirmed’ his fear but does not show a causal influence from strategies to appraisals.
No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies cause or lead to triggers; triggers appear without being caused by strategies.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that triggers (e.g., car backfiring, police presence) cause or lead to negative appraisals (e.g., ‘he could not cope’).
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals cause or lead to intrusive memory; the memory intrudes without being driven by appraisals.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals cause or lead to triggers; triggers appear independently.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies (avoidance, checking) cause or lead to negative appraisals; the text says strategies ‘confirmed’ his fear but does not show a causal influence from strategies to appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies cause or lead to triggers; triggers appear without being caused by strategies.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
